He and his wife are bathed with water from eight kinds of grain and herbs, then enter the sacrificial hall by the west door with sons and grandsons. After honouring the obstacle-remover, the Ganga and Yamuna, he sits, drives away harmful spirits, honours his seat and the Earth, and starts the worship. A long section gives the forms to be pictured and the offerings for Varuna the water god, the sun, moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn and the two shadow planets, the guardians of the eight directions, Brahma, Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha, Lakshmi, the goddess Ambika killing the buffalo demon, Earth, Vishvakarma and Sarasvati. Chants and sacred hymns to be recited are listed, as are fire offerings. After bathing the sponsor and a sacred post, a formal gift of the water to all beings is made in a set sentence, fish and turtles are put in, and the pond is honoured and circled. The sponsor gives gold, cows and food to the priests, and returns home to feed Brahmins, children and the poor.

03-020.json.summary: Suta begins with a note that the rite just described is the best, middle and lower versions giving middle and lower fruit, and says he will now give the middle form, for those of average means. The post and other items are made ready the day before. The chapter repeats the choice of a worthy priest, lists persons to avoid (for example the wifeless, the childless and a priest who serves crowds), and gives short prayers to the teacher. The sponsor and his wife enter the hall, and the pots, altar and the nine-pot layout for Varuna, Brahma, Vasudeva and the guardians are described, with the musical measure for each deity, and the food offering for each planet. Eight great serpents, such as Ananta, Vasuki and Takshaka, are made in metals and honoured with offerings. Fire offerings, bathing of the sponsor, planting of the post, offering of gifts, and the setting of Varuna into the pond with fish, birds and turtles follow. The gift of the water to all beings is repeated, with fees to priests and a feast for Brahmins, children and the poor.

04-001.json.summary: The Madhyama Parva, third part, begins. Suta says he will now teach the special rules for gardens and similar works. A square, level area is marked out, with a pot for the god in the north-east, a middle pot for the planets, and Varuna in the centre. Vasudeva (Vishnu) is to be pictured in the centre of the lotus, four-armed with conch, discus, mace and lotus, attended by Lakshmi and Pushti, and worshipped with the usual offerings. The moon, Indra, Shiva and others are given places, and a table of fire offerings is given for each. The fire's seven tongues are named. The chapter ends with the ear-piercing of the trees with a needle (a rite for newly planted trees), gifts to the teacher and priests, and rules for bridge and causeway works, including laying five jewels in a hole and planting banana trees by the bridge. Another ritual verse notes that a person who falls from a tree is not stained by sin.

04-002.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, gives the rite for dedicating a cow-pasture (gopracara). Vishnu with Lakshmi, Brahma, Rudra, Varaha, the sun, moon and Mahadeva are worshipped, fire offerings are made, and a post with serpent hoods is planted. The giver then says the verse of gift: a jewel is placed in the ground and the land is given to the cows. The text promises freedom from sin and a stay in Vishnu's world for as many thousand years as there are blades of grass; it also says one who digs up or ploughs a pasture ruins his family and incurs the guilt of killing a Brahmin. A "cow-hide" of land is defined as the area where a hundred cows and one bull graze freely. The chapter then describes the rite for a roadside shelter (mandapa) for travellers, with prayers to the guardians of the directions, and for a well, with the eight serpent kings invoked by name. It closes with the rite for a garden, which includes piercing the trees' ears, a formal gift sentence, the same verse about falling from a tree, and gifts to priests.

04-003.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, describes the dedication of a small garden. On a level plot, a pot is set up and Vishnu and the moon are worshipped; one teacher is chosen; the trees are wrapped with thread, garlanded and given their "wish" offering, and five Brahmins are fed. The ears of the trees are pierced, the garden is formally given away, a post is set up in the middle and banana plants in the directions. Fire offerings and the fee follow. The chapter ends with the rule for a single tree: worship of Dharma, Earth, the guardians and others at its foot, a cow as fee, and water offered to the sun.

04-004.json.summary: Suta describes the rite of installing a pipal (ashvattha) tree, and, in the same chapter, a pond. A square of ground is prepared at the foot of the tree, a lotus is drawn, a pot is set up the night before, three Brahmins are fed, and the tree is wrapped in white thread. Ganesha, Brahma, the guardians of the directions and the nine planets are worshipped. Shiva is pictured as a white, two-armed figure with a trident, seated on a bull, and honoured with the usual offerings and fire offerings. The text then turns to the dedication of a pond, with the water god Varuna made in silver, a serpent figure of Ananta, and a set of fire offerings. The sponsor says a formal sentence to give the pond to Brahmins for the use of all beings, boats are used, and fish and turtles are released. Fees, milk poured round the pond, and kindness to the poor close the rite.

04-005.json.summary: Suta gives the rule for installing a lotus-pond, a step-well or a lake, and then for a garden or a single tree. The place is prepared the day before, Ganesha, Varuna, Shiva, Vishnu and others are worshipped, and fire offerings and food gifts are made. The sponsor sets up a post and gives a cow as fee, then offers water to the sun. The garden rite then begins: a round hall and a square fire pit in a forest to the west or north, with Vishvaksena and Vasudeva (Vishnu) pictured with two consorts, the moon, Vanaspati (lord of trees) and a series of fire offerings. Water is mixed with Ganga water and herbs, the sponsor is bathed with prayers, and the teacher and Brahmins are given a cow, a metal vessel and fees.

04-006.json.summary: This short chapter repeats, almost word for word, the rite for a small garden given in chapter 260: a pot is set in a prepared place, Vishnu and the moon are worshipped, trees are wrapped and garlanded, five Brahmins are fed, the ears of the trees are pierced, and the garden is formally given. A post is put in the middle with banana plants in the directions, and fire offerings and the fee follow. The chapter ends with the usual closing line giving it as the sixth chapter of the third part.

04-007.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, gives the rite for one or a few chosen trees, almost as in chapter 260. A pot is set on the west side of the tree, the tree is wrapped with thread, and Brahma, the moon, Vishnu and Vanaspati (lord of trees) are worshipped. Fire offerings of sesame and barley are made, the post is given with a banana plant, and Dharma, Earth, the guardians and attendant spirits are honoured at the tree's foot. A cow is given as fee and water is offered to the sun. This chapter is very short.

04-008.json.summary: Suta gives again the rite for installing a pipal (ashvattha) tree, a shorter form of chapter 261. A square of ground is marked with sandalwood at the foot of the tree and a lotus drawn on it. The night before, a pot is set up and three Brahmins are fed. Ganesha, Brahma, the guardians of the directions and the planets are worshipped, then Shiva is placed in the circle with his attendants Chanda, Pracanda, Nandi and Bhringi, Ananta, Kama and Ganesha, and Kartikeya in the middle. Shiva is pictured as a white two-armed figure with a trident, and Vishnu is worshipped at the foot and Brahma at the top. Food offerings and fire offerings for Rudra follow, a banana plant is set up, and the teacher is satisfied with gifts. The rite ends with milk poured in five streams and water offered to the sun.

04-009.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, gives a very short rule for dedicating a banyan tree. At its foot, on the south side, a three-hand altar is made with three pots, and Ganesha, Shiva and Vishnu are worshipped. A rice-and-milk offering is cooked, red threads and gold are used, a barley-and-milk food-offering is given, and the tree is formally given away with spoken words. The post is planted and bound with banyan roots, and the chapter ends in a list of yakshas, nagas, gandharvas, siddhas and wind-gods, apparently those to be honoured. The text is cut short.

04-010.json.summary: Suta describes the dedication of a bilva tree, the tree sacred to Shiva. The night before, a pot is set up and the tree is made ready, and the rite follows an eight-petal drawing at the foot and the binding of the tree with red threads. Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma, Durga, Kubera and others are worshipped, with fire offerings of sesame, food offerings to yakshas, twelve gifts of cakes and a fee including gold and a bronze vessel. Seven Brahmins and a couple are fed, the post is planted, the tree's ears are pierced, and water is offered to the sun. Suta then gives a night version of the rite, saying that one who performs the single-tree rite is not born again on earth. It ends with pots, milk and cow-products, a feast for a Brahmin couple and the fee of grain and a cow.

04-011.json.summary: Suta states a short promise: a person who makes a plot of land a hundred hands in size, planted with trees and with betel-nut and mango fruits, and worships there, lives in heaven for sixty thousand years. He then gives the rule in brief, which is to complete the daily rites, honour five Brahmins and feed them, worship Vishnu together with Prajapati, make the fire offering and give a fee to a Brahmin. The chapter is very short and gives no more detail.

04-012.json.summary: Suta gives the rite of dedicating a hall (mandapa) built of stone, wood, grass or straw. On the evening before, a pot is set up at an auspicious hour, and the sun, moon and Vishnu are worshipped in it, with sprinkling of water, scent, oil, sandal, vermilion and eye-black. At dawn the growth-rite for ancestors is done, the guardians of the directions are placed, and Ganesha, the planets and the sun are worshipped with a fire offering of milk-rice. The hall is then formally given to Brahmins and all beings, with the words of gift given in the text, and a white pot is set on top, with the hall wrapped in thread and water. A fee is given and water is offered to the sun. A further note covers a shelter for water-giving, where Varuna and Vishvakarma are worshipped, and says that the flag alone is enough when nothing else can be done.

04-013.json.summary: Suta describes the rite of consecrating a well with a great post, four hands high and sixteen hands long, over three nights. Varuna is set in a white pot on the west of the well, and the bathing, scent, oil, flower, incense, cloth and food-offering mantras are given. No ancestral rite is done at the start; it is done at the end. A couple is fed, one Brahmin is chosen, and Varuna is worshipped with Narayana, Shiva and Earth. Ten fire offerings go to Varuna and one each to the others, with the names of Shiva (Shankara, Rudra, Sharva, Pashupati, Ugra, Bhava, Mahadeva, Ishana) in a food-offering. The well is given with a spoken sentence in which the giver says he is doing it for his father, and a milch cow and fee follow. A short rule for a small well in a hall closes the chapter.

04-014.json.summary: Suta describes the dedication of a flower garden. A three-hand altar is made in the middle, a pot is set up, and the day before the Brahmins are fed. Ganesha, the sun, the moon, Agni and Narayana are worshipped. A milk-rice and honey offering is made, the post is planted in the north-east, the ears of the plants are pierced, and wheat is sprinkled. A fee of grain, barley and wheat is given to a Brahmin, and the garden is bound round with water poured in many streams. The chapter is very short.

04-015.json.summary: Suta describes the rite for installing a tulasi (holy basil) plant, to be done in the months Jyeshtha and Ashadha, on a pure day or on the eleventh lunar day. The night before, a pot is set up and Narayana, Shiva, the moon, Brahma and Indra are worshipped, with a list of mantras for scent, oil, flowers, sandal, grass, mirror, fruit and eye-black. Women who are devoted to their husbands bathe the plant. After the ancestral rite and the choice of the teacher as priest, a ten-hand hall is prepared and Narayana is worshipped with the planets, the world-guardians, Adityas, Maruts, Rudras and Vasus. A fire offering of sesame and barley is made, a post and banana plants are set up, and a fee including gold, a milch cow and a pouring of milk follows. The chapter ends with a list of trees for which this installation, or the piercing of ears, is not to be done, for example the jayanti, kadamba, neem, pipal-like trees, the shalmali and the khadira.

04-016.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, says the dedication of trees and similar works can be done in the best, middle or lower form. This chapter gives the rite for a bridge or causeway (setu). A round or square area is marked, a pot is set up the night before, and Earth and Shiva are worshipped. Scent, sandal, grass, fruit, cloth and eye-black are offered with mantras, and the ancestral rite is done the next day. A teacher and a main priest are chosen, with extra priests for large rites. Vishnu as Shesha and as the boar, Varaha, is worshipped, with fire offerings in sets and food offerings. The giver says a set sentence: he gives the bridge to Vishnu to raise twenty-one generations of his family to heaven. A verse says that if people fall in the mud or are hurt at the bridge, he is not to be stained by sin, and he gives away the merit of building it. A post and flags, a fee and a feast for relatives follow, and a shorter form for a small bridge is added.

04-017.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, goes on with the gift of grazing land. Someone who gives a square plot of sixty hands for cows to graze lives sixty thousand years in the world of Rudra, with smaller rewards for half, a quarter or an eighth, or for giving land, a maiden, a slave-girl or a bull. A cow given without ornaments earns half the fruit. The place is prepared, Brahma, Indra, Ganesha, the field guardian and the guardians of the directions are worshipped, a post is set and the ground is given with a sentence of gift. The text repeats that the giver is freed from sin, goes to Vishnu's world and stays there for as many thousand years as there are blades of grass on the land.

04-018.json.summary: Suta explains that in the present age (Kali), a person of small means can do a dedication in one day, by making the god dwell in the image at once, using clarified butter. The rite should begin after the sun turns north and after autumn, in spring. A set of thirty-two forms of Narayana and others, and images such as the elephant-faced Ganesha, may be installed. The sponsor does his daily rites, then the growth-rite, feeds Brahmins and goes to the sacrificial hall. Ganesha, the planets and the guardians are worshipped in pots, and Vishnu with his attendants on a prepared ground. The image is bathed with five kinds of water, with the five nectars, the five cow products, five kinds of earth, oils, decoctions and flower waters. The breath of life is invoked in the image, a fire offering is made, and the fee is given. This chapter is short.

04-019.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the Brahmins, goes on to the installation of images of the goddesses such as Kali and Tara. The place is made ready the day before, the ancestral growth-rite is done, and the goddess Durga is worshipped in a pot and then at a bilva tree, with the breath of life called into the image. The rule for images of Kali and Tara is that the image is bathed for three days, worshipped morning and night in a copper pot, and then placed in a chest with food offerings, animal gifts and fire offerings on the eighth day. Next he turns to the installation of the Shiva lingam, with the usual choices of teacher and priests, bathing, worship with attendants, and a gift of a cow of sesame or gold. Then a stone for a household shrine is installed on the twelfth lunar day and installation rules are given for images of the sun, Ganesha, Brahma, the boar-goddess and many forms of the goddess. The chapter ends with a three-day rite with girl worship, fire offerings, animal gifts where means allow, and a night of waking at the monastery festival.

04-020.json.summary: Suta, speaking to the sages, begins the teaching on bad omens and their remedies. Omens are divided into three kinds: those of the sky, of the air, and of the earth. Examples given include meteors, fire in the sky, halos, dryness of tanks, gods seen laughing or weeping or bleeding, falling stones in rain, earthquakes, comets, eclipses, birds like owls entering a house, snakes or frogs appearing in pots, lightning striking a house, strange growth of plants, and cows behaving oddly. For each, the text says what harm may follow, to the household, the king, the ministers or the country, and the remedy, a fire offering of ten thousand oblations on a day linked to the planet concerned (sun, moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu and the comet), a cooked offering, and a gift of a cow, gold or cloth to a Brahmin. The last part gives the number of fire offerings for each planet and day in a three-day rite. The last verse gives a verse count in an unclear way and says the Bhavishya would then be complete.

05-001.json.summary: The Pratisarga Parva (the "history" part) begins with a prayer to Narayana, Nara, the goddess Sarasvati and Vyasa. Shaunaka asks Suta which kings ruled in the twenty-eighth Satya age of the Vaivasvata period, and for the length of their reigns. Suta answers with a list of the sun-line kings, beginning with Vaivasvata Manu, whose son was Ikshvaku, born after a hundred years of penance on the Sarayu river. The chapter names a long series of kings and gives each a rule of thousands of years, shortening step by step: Vikukshi, Kakutstha, Prithu, Yuvanashva, Mandhata, Purukutsa, Trishanku, Harishchandra, Rohita, Sagara and others down to Sudarshana. It notes which kings were devoted to Vishnu and which to Shiva, and mentions Sagara's sons, Bhagiratha, Ambarisha, Kalmashapada, and Khatvanga's help to Indra. Sudarshana, who is devoted to the goddess, wins the Kashi king's daughter, and rules five thousand years. Then the great goddess Mahakali tells him in a dream to go with his wife and with Vasishtha and others to the Himalaya, as a great wind will destroy the land of Bharata and its seas and islands within seven years. He goes with leading kings, merchants and Brahmins. The chapter then describes the world drying and changing over about five to ten years, until the ground appears again as dry land.

05-002.json.summary: Suta continues the story. On the third day of the bright half of Vaishakha, a Thursday, Sudarshana returns to Ayodhya with the people, and by the goddess Maya's power the city is made splendid again. After ten thousand years of rule he reaches the eternal world, and his son Dilipa follows. The sun-line then runs through Raghu, Aja, Dasharatha and Rama (called Hari himself, whose reign is given as eleven thousand years), then Kusha, Atithi, Nala and many more, down to names such as Shakyavardhana, Prasenajit, Shudraka and Suratha. The text says the sixty-five kings of the Raghu line were devoted to the goddess and to animal sacrifice, and that the sons who were born then were of mixed classes. A second line follows from Chandra, sent by Indra, who ruled at Prayaga, with Budha, Pururava and Urvashi, Ayu, Nahusha (who became Indra and was cursed to be a snake by Durvasa), Yayati and his five sons, Yadu, and Pururava's descendants down to Samvarana. Samvarana does penance in the Himalaya and the sun, pleased, gives him the maiden Tapati; the king then goes to the sun's world. The text next says that by Maya's power the age reached its end: the four seas grew, then dried, and the land became dry again through Agastya's power. Samvarana is named at the end as coming back at the sun's order with Tapati, a sage and Vasishtha. The chapter is cut off here.

05-003.json.summary: Shaunaka asks Suta, here called Lomaharshana, when King Samvarana came back and who the kings of the Dvapara age were. Suta says that on the thirteenth of the dark half of Bhadra, on a Friday, Samvarana returned with the sages to Pratishthana, a fine city five yojanas long built by Vishvakarma. Other rulers were set up: one in the Yadu line at Mathura (Satvata), and one among the mleccha line in the desert country. A very long list of kings follows, mostly giving each a rule equal to or shorter than his father's, with many names formed from the sun, Brahma and moon. It includes Dushyanta and Shakuntala's son Bharata, from whom the land is said to be named Bharata, and Hastin, who founded Hastinapura on the Ganga. Kuru makes Kurukshetra, twenty yojanas wide, and the line runs through Shantanu, Vichitravirya, Pandu, Yudhishthira and Duryodhana, who is killed at Kurukshetra. The text says the demons killed in the old war with the gods were reborn in Shantanu's time, and that the earth, burdened by their armies, went to Indra, after which Hari was born as Krishna to Vasudeva and Devaki, lived one hundred and thirty-five years and went to Goloka. Kings after Abhimanyu's son follow, ending with Kshemaka, who leaves his kingdom, is killed by mlecchas and goes to the world of Yama. By Narada's advice, his son Pradyota does a mleccha sacrifice, in which the mlecchas are destroyed. The chapter ends there; the next explains the rite.

05-004.json.summary: Shaunaka asks how Pradyota did the sacrifice. Suta says that Narada came to Pradyota at Hastinapura, told him his father had been killed by mlecchas, and said a mleccha sacrifice would bring the father to heaven. Pradyota, angry, called Vedic Brahmins to Kurukshetra, made a square fire pit of sixteen yojanas, and by Vedic mantras burnt peoples such as the Hara-Hunas, Barbaras, Shakas, Khasas, Yavanas, Pahlavas, Chinas and others. Kshemaka went to heaven, and Pradyota, called "slayer of mlecchas", ruled ten thousand years; his son Vedavan followed. Kali, in the form of a mleccha, then praises Narayana, complaining that the Vedic king had destroyed his place. Hari appears and says he will take many forms to fulfil Kali's wish, naming a man Adama and his wife Havyavati, born of Vishnu and Kardama, to increase the mleccha line. Kali goes to Nilachala; the next king, Sunanda, dies childless, and the people of the Aryan land decline while mleccha lines grow. The sages of Naimisha, eighty-eight thousand of them, go to the Himalaya to worship Vishnu. Suta then tells the story of Adam and Havyavati: Kali, as a snake, deceives the wife in a forest east of the city of Pradana, they eat the fruit against Vishnu's command, cover themselves with fig leaves, and their children are mlecchas; Adam lives nine hundred and thirty years. His descendants follow (Shveta, Anuha, Kinasha, Mahallala, Virada, Hanuka and others), described as keeping some Vedic virtues. Nyuha, a devotee of Vishnu, is warned in a dream of a flood in seven days, builds a large boat, boards it with his family and all kinds of creatures, and survives forty days of rain that cover the land. The sages praise the goddess under many names, she calms the waters, and after a year the land dries; Nyuha, with his sons Sima, Shama and Bhava, lands near the Himalaya and settles.

05-005.json.summary: Shaunaka asks what has happened since the flood up to the present. Suta says that Nyuha, a mleccha, was deluded by Vishnu's illusion and his line grew; mleccha speech, turned away from the Vedic word, was made for him, and Nyuha's three sons are named as Sima, Hama and Yakuta. Their descendants and the lands named after them are listed in a general way, including Yakuta's seven sons and the four sons of Hama. Suta then falls into yogic sleep, and wakes after two thousand one hundred years to give the line of Sima: Sima rules five hundred years, followed by a line of sons with reigns of several hundred years each, which are named only in passing. The text says mleccha speech arose through Sarasvati's curse and is very low, while Sanskrit speech stays in Bharata. The sages at Vishala meditate on Nara-Narayana for two hundred years and are woken and ask about the present king. Suta says that, three thousand years into Kali, a king named Shankha rules in Avanti, and a Shaka lord rules in the mleccha land. He says that by Kali's second thousand the land was full of mlecchas, apart from Brahmavarta, that a mleccha teacher called Musha filled the world with his teachings, and he lists four kinds of mleccha speech and sample words. He adds that the holy seven cities see violence, that in mleccha lands the wise follow mleccha ways, and that mleccha rule is found in Bharata and its islands. He advises the sage to worship Hari, and the sages weep.

05-006.json.summary: Shaunaka asks why the mlecchas did not reach Brahmavarta. Suta says it is through Sarasvati's power. A Brahmin named Kashyapa, sent from heaven at the gods' order in the first thousand years of Kali, and his wife Aryavati had ten sinless sons, named by their learning or duties (for example Upadhyaya, Dikshita, Pathaka, Agnihotri, Dvivedi, Trivedi and Chaturvedi). Kashyapa goes to Kashmir and praises Sarasvati with red flowers, incense and food, asking her to make Sanskrit the best speech and to confuse the mlecchas. She is pleased; he goes to a land called Mishra, wins over the mlecchas, and makes ten thousand of them Brahmins, two thousand Vaishyas, and the rest Shudras. They live with him in the Aryan land, grow to four crore people, and he rules a hundred and twenty years. His son Magadha is made king, and from his time the Aryan land is divided into regions around Magadha. Shaunaka rejoices and later asks about the kings after Magadha. Suta lists the kings, from Shishunaga (born from a sacrifice as part of Balabhadra) through the Nanda line and Mahananda. Then, because Kali called to mind Hari, the text says Hari was born as Gautama, who changed to the Buddhist teaching and ruled at Pattana; Shakyamuni, Shuddhodana and Shakyasimha follow. The Vedic path is said to be destroyed and all people Buddhists. Buddhasimha, Chandragupta (who married the daughter of a Yavana ruler), Bindusara and Ashoka follow. At Mount Abu a Brahmin from Kanyakubja performs a fire rite, and four Kshatriyas (Pramara, Chapahani, Shukla and Parihara) are born from it, riding elephants, who overcome Ashoka and kill four lakh Buddhists with divine weapons. Pramara settles in Avanti at the city of Ambavati.

05-007.json.summary: Suta tells where the other three fire-born kings settled: Parihara at Kalinjara near Chitrakuta, where he rules as a destroyer of Buddhists; Chapahani at Ajmer in the land of Rajputs; and Shukla at Dvaraka in Anarta. The sages, asked to say more, are told by Suta that he is going into yogic sleep, and they meditate on Vishnu. After two thousand years he resumes: in Kali year 3,710 (as stated), Pramara rules six years, followed by his descendants and by Gandharvasena, who rules fifty years and then gives the kingdom to his son Shankha. A heavenly woman, Viramati, sent by Indra, bears Gandharvasena a son, and at his birth flowers fall from the sky and drums sound. A Brahmin named Shivadrishti, with disciples, goes to the forest, practises karma-yoga with twenty others and becomes Shiva. In the three-thousandth year of Kali, by Shiva's command, one born from Kailasa, to destroy the Shakas and increase Aryan dharma, is named Vikramaditya by his father. At five he goes to the forest for twelve years of penance, then goes to Ambavati; Shiva sends him a throne with thirty-two figures, and Parvati makes a spirit (Vaitala) to guard him. At Mahakaleshvara he worships Shiva, builds a hall, installs the throne, and listens to Brahmins. Vaitala, in the form of a Brahmin, offers to tell him a great tale. The chapter ends here.

06-001.json.summary: The Pratisarga Parva, second part, begins. Suta says that Vaitala, standing at Mahakaleshvara and thinking of Shiva, tells King Vikramaditya a tale. In Varanasi, King Pratapamukuta's son Vajramukuta, with Buddhidaksha, the minister's son, rides into a forest and sees a lake and a Shiva temple. There he sees Padmavati, daughter of King Dantavaktra of Karnata, and both faint. She takes a lotus from her hair, puts it to her ear, bites it with her teeth, puts it under her foot and then on her heart, and leaves. The prince goes silent with love. Buddhidaksha learns the cause, reads the signs as a message, and with the king's leave goes with him to Karnata. Through an old woman, Buddhidaksha sends messages, she is struck in rage, but he reads the blows and finger marks as signs to come at midnight by the west window. The prince meets her and stays a month. Wishing to see his friend, he asks her leave; she poisons the minister's son's food, but he feeds it to a dog, which dies. The prince, now wary of women's tricks, leaves her, but Buddhidaksha advises him to take her ornaments while she sleeps, mark her knee with a trident, and leave. As a yogi he sells the ornament, the prince is seized as a thief, and the yogi tells the king he saw her as a pishachi in a cremation ground and marked her knee. The king drives out his daughter, and Vajramukuta takes her home. Vaitala asks who gets the great sin; Vikramaditya says the king, because the minister acted for his friend, the guards for their master, and the prince for his goal. He adds rules: a man who does not marry a daughter who has reached puberty goes to hell for sixty thousand years; one who hinders a gandharva marriage is punished by Yama; one who abandons a faultless girl goes to hell for a lakh of years.

06-002.json.summary: Suta says the pleased Vaitala tells a second tale. In Dharmasthala on the Yamuna, King Gunadhipa rules, and his priest Harisharma has a son Satyashila and a daughter Madhumati. When she is twelve, three Brahmins, Vamana, Trivikrama and Keshava, are each chosen for her by her father, brother and herself, and the wedding is fixed for the thirteenth of the dark half of Magha, on a Friday. At that time she is bitten by a snake and dies. Trivikrama becomes a wandering ascetic, Keshava gathers her bones and goes to holy sites, and Vamana stays by her pyre, taking the ashes. Trivikrama, at a house on the Sarayu, sees Ramasharma bring a dead boy back to life with a life-giving mantra, and receives the mantra. He goes to the Yamuna, revives the girl, and also the dead son of King Gunadhipa, who offers a boon; Trivikrama asks him to find Keshava, who brings the bones. When she is revived, she says she will go to the man who is right for her by dharma, and the three stand silent. Vaitala asks who is right for her. Vikramaditya answers that she is right for Vamana: the one who gave life is like a father, and the one who gave the bones is like a brother. The chapter ends on that answer.

06-003.json.summary: Vaitala tells a third tale, and Suta calls it charming. In Vardhavan, King Rupasena and Queen Vidvanmala have as servant a warrior, Viravara, who comes with his wife, son and daughter and receives a thousand gold pieces daily, half of which he spends on fire rites, holy places and Brahmins. After a year, the goddess Royal Fortune (Rajalakshmi), on Shiva's order, weeps in a cemetery at midnight to test them. The king sends Viravara to find out. She says she is Rupasena's fortune, that the king will die in a month, and that he can live long if Viravara's son's head is offered to Chandika. Viravara's wife, son and daughter all agree; the son asks to be offered, Viravara cuts off his head, and his daughter, wife and he himself die. Seeing this, the king offers his own head. The goddess, pleased, revives all and grants the king a boon, and he asks that Viravara and his family live. The king gives his daughter Kamarupini to Viravara's son. Vaitala asks who showed the best love; the answer given is that the king did, offering his body for a servant, while the servant loved gold, the wife followed duty, the sister loved her kin and the son loved his father.

06-004.json.summary: Suta tells how Vaitala continues with a fourth tale. In the city of Bhogavati, King Rupavarma keeps a wise parrot, Chudamani, who tells him, when he is thirty and asks for a bride, that Chandravati, daughter of the king of Magadha, is right for him. A Brahmin named Ganesha is sent with gifts to arrange it. He praises Shiva, and Chandravati, with her friend the female myna Madanamanjari (Menaka), prays to Durga, who confuses her parents and has the wedding done within a month. Later the king tells Menaka to marry the parrot. She refuses with a story of a wicked merchant's son, Madapala, who gambled and drank, lost everything, married the daughter of a rich man by lying, then killed his servant and abandoned his wife, and later killed her too for her ornaments; so she says some matches are unfit. The parrot in turn refuses to marry a lowly, dark female and tells a story of Jayalakshmi, wife of Shridatta, who took a lover, Homadatta, while her husband was away trading; when Homadatta died of snakebite, a spirit in a pipal tree entered his body and bit off her nose, and the thief Kaphalla saw it. The king, told by the thief, put her on a donkey and sent her to the forest. Vaitala asks who is more sinful, the woman or the man. Vikramaditya's answer, as given, is that Maya takes three forms (male, female, neuter) from Brahman, that women are bound more by action, and that action binds while knowledge frees; so he declares the woman more sinful and the man less.

06-005.json.summary: Suta tells a fifth tale from Vaitala. King Mahabala of Ujjayini has a messenger, Haridasa, a devotee of Hari, whose daughter Mahadevi asks to be given to a man better than her father. Sent to King Harishchandra of Telangana, Haridasa tells him about the coming of Kali. He says Nyuha's time came first, that Om came from Brahma's mouth and many deluding languages from the second mouth for Kali's sake, and that Kali's rule is known when Vedic dharma is turned upside down and mlecchas are loved. He describes Kali's family (Falsehood as wife, Misery as son, Bad Fate as his half), kings ruled by anger, Brahmins ruled by desire, the rich by greed, Shudras gaining greatness, shameless women and servants who kill masters, and a barren earth; he says those who take refuge in Hari are glad. Harishchandra gives him gifts. A Brahmin shows Haridasa an aerial vehicle given by the goddess, and Haridasa promises him his daughter. Mukunda, Haridasa's son, is told by his teacher to give his sister to the teacher's son. Mahadevi herself chooses Vamana, a pupil of Drona's son who shoots by sound, so three Brahmins come for her. A rakshasa carries her to the Vindhya mountain; one Brahmin (an astrologer) says where she is, one carries the other two in his vehicle, and the archer kills the rakshasa by sound. They bring her back, and then quarrel over her. Vikramaditya's answer is that the one who found her is like a father, the one who carried them like a brother, and the one who killed the rakshasa is right for the girl.

06-006.json.summary: Suta tells a sixth tale from Vaitala. In Dharmapura, the good King Dharmashila and Queen Lajjadevi have a minister, Andhaka. The king builds a temple to Durga, holds a festival for a child, and Durga appears at midnight and offers a boon; he praises her as the one eternal Prakriti by whom Vishnu, Brahma and all beings act. A voice says he will have a mighty son. A washerman, Kalibhojana, with his friend Kashidasa, sees a girl, Kamangi, walking with her father and, mad with desire, promises Chandika his head if he gets her. The goddess confuses the father and the marriage is made. After a year, Kalibhojana goes to the temple and offers his head; Kashidasa, out of love, offers his, and Kamangi, in grief, offers hers. Chandika revives all three and grants a boon: Kashidasa asks for Kamangi, Kamangi asks for her husband, and Kalibhojana asks for his friend's fine body. Vaitala asks what the goddess did; the answer given is that the heads of the two men had been cut off and she put them the wrong way round, and each received his own boon.

06-007.json.summary: Suta tells a seventh tale from Vaitala. In Champapuri, King Champakesha and Queen Sulochana have a daughter, Trilokasundari, whose beauty is praised. At her svayamvara, kings arrive, and Indra, Yama, Kubera and Varuna come in human form. Four men claim her: one says he is Indradatta, skilled in all the scriptures; another, Dharmadatta, skilled in archery; a third, Dhanapala, who knows the speech of all living things; and a fourth, skilled in the arts, who each day earns five jewels, which he gives to merit, to the fire rite, to himself, to his wife and for good food. The king is bewildered and asks his daughter, but she is shy and does not answer. Vaitala asks whom she should marry. Vikramaditya says Dharmadatta, giving the reasoning: the scripture-skilled man is a Brahmin by class, the language-knower a merchant, the arts-skilled a Shudra and the archer a king, and a girl is always fit for a man of her own class. She is then married to the good Dharmadatta.

06-008.json.summary: Suta tells an eighth tale from Vaitala. In Mithilavati in the Videha land, King Gunadhipa takes in a Kshatriya, Chiramdeva, who settles there for a living. Out hunting, the king kills a tiger and, lost in the forest, hungry and thirsty, is fed by Chiramdeva with cooked deer meat. The king offers him a boon; Chiramdeva asks that a thousand coins be given to him in turn and a hundred each month for his family. Later the king sends him to the sea, where he finds the goddess Kusumada, a gandharva's daughter at Markandeya's place, and asks to marry her. She tells him to bathe in her pool; he is swept back to Mithila and reports it to the king. The king goes to the temple, and the goddess asks him to take her in a gandharva marriage, saying she was cursed to give pleasure to a man. The king refuses, says he treats Chiramdeva like a son, and asks her to be his wife; she becomes like a daughter-in-law to him. Vaitala asks whose truth and duty was the greatest. Vikramaditya answers that Chiramdeva's was the greatest: he served the king faithfully with no other living, and the king saw it in a time of need.

06-009.json.summary: Suta tells a ninth tale from Vaitala, who finds Vikramaditya very capable. In Kamapura, King Virasimha rules justly. The merchant Hiranyadatta's daughter Kamalasa is touched by Somadatta in a forest; she says she is a maiden, promises to come to him on the tenth day after her wedding, and he lets her go. She is married to the merchant's son Madapala. On the ninth day her husband, in desire, embraces her; she weeps, tells him the promise, and he gives her leave. She goes at night; a thief stops her for her ornaments, and she promises to give them after she meets her lover. Somadatta, moved by Vishnu, honours her as a faithful wife and sends her away; the thief, too, let her keep them and returns her to her husband's house. Vaitala asks whose truthfulness was best, and Vikramaditya answers: the thief's. The merchant acted out of fear of the king, she out of fear of widowhood, her husband out of fear of dharma, and the thief out of fear of untruth.

06-010.json.summary: Suta tells of the dutiful king Gunashekhara. Once he goes to Shiva's temple and a scorpion stings him in anger. A fearless man draws the poison out, and speaks about six inner enemies: delusion, pride, arrogance, possessiveness, desire and blame. He says that Vishnu, Rudra and Brahma are bound by illusion, and that the true Jina, who is non-dual and spotless, is not conquered. He teaches worship of the cow, no harm to creatures, and no meat or drink, and the king takes up the Jain way. His grieving queen takes refuge in Shiva and by Rudra's boon bears a fine son. Gunashekhara dies and goes to hell, while his father gets heaven by his son's duty. The king is later at ease in spring with his queens, and a wife faints when he hands her a lotus. The story ends with the Vedic duty being named as the chief one and the householder living like an ascetic being praised in the Jain books.

06-011.json.summary: Suta tells of Punyapura, where the minister is Satyaprakasha. The king asks how many kinds of joy exist, and is told that the joy of a student is Brahma's joy, that of a forest-dweller is a lesser joy of duty, and that of a renouncer is Shiva's joy, the best. He says there is no joy without a wife in the householder's life, and tells his minister to look for a fitting woman. The minister goes from place to place and finds a girl sitting on a golden tree in the water. The king goes to the sea shore and tells her he has come for her. She says on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight a Rakshasa with a crane vehicle will take her. The king kills the Rakshasa and she says she is the daughter of a Vidyadhara. A great festival follows in the city. It ends with the saying that a king who is a sensualist ruins his kingdom.

06-012.json.summary: Suta tells that Devasvami, a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, worshipped Shiva for a son, and a strong boy named Harisvami was born with a share of the gods. His wife, Rupalavanyika, is as lovely as a goddess. Once in spring with her husband, a Gandharva called Sukala is taken by her beauty. The husband wakes and searches for her, then gives up all sense objects and meditates on Hari. Under a banyan tree an ascetic comes, eats milk-rice that was poisoned and dies, going to Shiva's world. Vetala asks the king who bears the sin of killing a Brahmin. The king answers that a Brahmin gave alms to a hungry man out of fate's confusion, that a person must always suffer the sin he has done himself, and that the sin falls on the one who gave the poison.

06-013.json.summary: Suta tells of a merchant named Dharmadhvaja and a man-eating Rakshasa named Vashara. A pleased Rakshasa speaks to his devotee. A pit is made that confuses men's minds, and a thief steals from the king's house at night and hides the goods in the pit. The guards are deluded by the Rakshasa woman's magic. A man says he is a thief and offers the king a share. At midnight the thief tells the king to go home, as the Rakshasa will eat all men that night. The king brings his wealth and the women. The thief is paraded through the town on a donkey with drumbeats and is to be impaled. The king's daughter, deluded by divine illusion, appears, and the goddess Durga is pleased and revives both. The king explains why the man wept and then laughed.

06-014.json.summary: Suta tells of Chandraprabha, a lovely wife who goes to a flowery wood with her friends and is entranced, and a Brahmin who falls to the ground. A Brahmin sees the beautiful young woman and tells her sorrow to another. A twelve-year-old girl is named. Sudeva, a fine Brahmin, is always in her heart, and he tells her that if she is meant for the best Brahmin, a child will come in four months. A minister's son, deluded by a woman's form, embraces her. A minister named Rajakara has a son Madanalasa. The king gives the bride with wealth by Vedic rule, and Shashi takes the king's daughter home. Vetala asks the king whom the girl belongs to, and the king answers that a field belongs to the farmer and not to the seed-giver. Madanalasa then praises Govinda with a hymn, is freed, and embraces his wife joyfully.

06-015.json.summary: Suta tells of a generous Brahmin at Kanyakubja who asks what to do about his poverty. By the goddess's grace a son named Jimutaketu becomes lord of the Vidyadharas and lives for years in divine pleasures. In an earlier life he was a king in the middle country who hunted, kept a night vigil in Valmiki's hut and heard the story of Rama. A tree speaks to him. On the Malaya mountain a girl called Kamalakshi lives at a Shiva temple, and Jimutavahana, struck by love at the sight of her, prays to the god of love. He is given Vishvavasu as a prince. Jimutavahana weeps where an old woman is grieving for her son who is to be eaten by Garuda. Garuda takes him through the sky, and the girl sees him in the air. Garuda hears him say he came to save the old woman's son, and the god vanishes. Vetala puts a question, and the story ends with Shankhachuda going against his enemy.

06-016.json.summary: Suta tells of a merchant, Ratnadatta, who knows duty and is rich. Seeing a woman's lovely form, he says to the king: "Take her, ocean of kindness, she is made fit for you." King Chandrashekhara, called to counsel his minister Vidura, goes home. He worships with incense, lamps and flowers, and a woman wails in fear. He kills a tiger and rejoices. He goes to the temple of Kamavaruthini, whose image will bring delusion on the king, so he does not marry. A woman who was Balabhadra's wife is named. The king, struck by Kama's arrow, faints and falls. A man says the woman is the daughter of Ratnadatta and the wife of his servant, fit for the king. The angry king says he would go to hell if he took her. The army chief is burnt to ashes. Vetala asks whose merit is greater, and the answer is that the king who conquers desire and keeps duty is greater.

06-017.json.summary: Suta tells of King Mahasena of Ujjayini. His son Gunakara loves wine and meat, is abandoned by his relatives and wanders the earth. A yogi, Kapardin, honours him with a meal from skulls, and calls a Yakshini for hospitality. In the morning she goes to Kailasa. Kapardin teaches him the knowledge that draws a Yakshini. He recites the mantra but the lovely goddess does not come. He lives at home with his parents at night, then goes to Pratibodhi's forest and becomes his pupil. He asks why his beloved Yakshini was not obtained. The answer is that action for success is of three kinds, of the body, of speech and of mind, all three together bring success in this life, and so seekers should do all three. The sage praises him.

06-018.json.summary: Suta tells of a just and generous man devoted to Shiva, and his lovely daughter Dhanavati. In time her daughter Mohini is born, and Dhanavati, widowed and without money, lives at her father's house. A Brahmin named Nyayasharma, who stole a Brahmin's property, is mentioned. A merchant's daughter touches the hand of a man who cries out for Rama, Krishna, Pradyumna and Aniruddha. A Brahmin says he is on the stake for three days. Dhanavati marries her daughter Mohini to him, and he dies and goes to Yama's world. Mohini, young and at her mother's house, is told a verse by a Brahmin asking who sleeps and who wakes, and the Brahmins cannot answer. A kindly sage tells her that beings die and are born every day, and describes how desire arises from resolve and greed from desire. Shiva instructs a king who wants a son. A child with three hands is born and the king is amazed. Vetala says a learned man who wants money is like a teacher.

06-019.json.summary: Suta tells of King Rupadatta of Chitrakuta. At noon on a lake shore, a sage's son sees a girl, their eyes meeting, and the king gains knowledge at the sight. A wise sage tells the king duty that includes compassion: take punishment from the unworthy and gain the fruit of worshipping the worthy, truth in worship of the gods, self-control in worship of the teacher. The sage gives his daughter to the king and goes home. A Rakshasa wants to eat the king's wife and asks for a seven-year-old Brahmin boy to be given for him. The boy laughs loudly at the time of death. The middle son, knowing this, takes refuge in the king, and a Shiva devotee laughs when he sees the king with a sword in hand. Vetala asks why.

06-020.json.summary: Suta tells a Vetala story of a village merchant, Arthadatta, who is busy in trade and gives his daughter in marriage to a merchant named Suvarna. By chance a fine Brahmin comes to the house of Anangamanjari. After a fire offering, a lovely woman's daughter goes to clean, and the girl, her eyes unsteady with passion, gives the Brahmin an appointment. At midnight she waits for him, but by fate he does not come, and she dies. The Brahmin, seeing her lifeless, also dies. Suvarna comes and weeps for his beloved. Vetala asks the king, who answers that a Brahmin is always to be honoured by the merchant class as the form of Brahman, and that Suvarna understood in his heart that his beloved was devoted to Brahmins.

06-021.json.summary: Vetala tells King Vikrama a humble tale. A Brahmin learned in the Vedas lives in a village and has four sons, each given to one of the four parts of life. By fate they lose their wealth, and ask their father why. He tells them gambling spends wealth and is the root of sin, tells one son to leave the company of courtesans and to give up meat and wine, and tells them all to turn to Lord Vishnu and give up unbelief and abuse of the gods. They go to another holy place, and after a year Shiva gives them the knowledge that revives the dead. They find a dead tiger's bones. One casts mantra-blessed water on them, the other pours milk, one pours water, and the unbeliever gives water to the sleeping tiger. Vetala asks who is the greatest fool, and the answer is the one who woke the tiger.

06-022.json.summary: Vetala tells of a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and has two sons skilled in all learning. An old man devoted to Shiva, Shambhudatta, makes a joyful fire offering. Liladhara sees a goat about to die and says killing creatures leads to a dreadful hell. He recalls that long ago in the Satya age, Brahmins performed sacrifices and spoke sweetly, but their view gave no fruit. The sages are amazed. In the Treta age the world became full of rajas, and he says gods are pleased by offerings, not by flesh and blood. A king named Kshatrasimha comes to Mohana, who tells of reciting the Saptashati and the goddess who creates and protects the world, and lists her powers such as Shachi, Siddhi, thirst, contentment, love, conduct, harm and patience. Kshatrasimha is tested by questions. The chapter says this is the time of Vikrama's story, and that a king will restore the holy places. Vetala vanishes and tells the sages, headed by Suta, that twilight has come.

06-023.json.summary: Vyasa tells that the sages lived in deep trance for a year. At that time King Vikramaditya is mentioned. The sages go to Suta and propose to have the king perform a horse sacrifice by his command. Suta comes with them. The horse goes to Kapila's place in the east and the bridge to Lanka in the south, and then to the Kshipra river. All the gods with their wives come to the king's sacrifice. After it the king gives many gifts, together with Vetala, and the moon gives nectar water and vanishes. The king gives the nectar to Indra, who goes to heaven. A Brahmin named Jayanta praises Bhartrihari for a hundred thousand gold pieces, and Vikramaditya rules without thorns. Shaunaka and the sages, knowing the king reached heaven, hear Suta recite the Puranas again.

06-024.json.summary: Vyasa asks Suta for something for people's good across the four ages. Suta begins with a salutation to Rama with Lakshmana and Sita. Once the yogi Narada, wishing to help others, sees the sufferings of people in the Kali age and asks how their sorrow may surely end. He goes to the white, four-armed Narayana, who is calm, cheerful and praised by Sanaka and others. Narada says that duty has four feet with truth as its ornament, and the best means is the Satya Narayana vow, and asks what the fruit and rule are. The Lord says that by it a person bound is freed, a fearful one becomes fearless. One bathes in the morning, is pure, takes a tooth-stick, resolves "I will keep your vow", and worships in the evening, with Shaligrama and gold, and recites the six-chapter story. The offering is divided between the teacher and the family, and Brahmins are fed. Narada then goes to heaven.

06-025.json.summary: Suta tells of the famous city of Kashi and an excellent but poor Brahmin there. Narayana appears to a gentle, humble man and says "by my advice, worship Satya Narayana". The Brahmin, instructed by the kind Hari, praises him with a hymn, describing him in a yellow garment with lotus eyes. The Lord gives the rule: with little effort and simple faith one worships, offering wheat flour with ghee, Ganga water with honey and the five nectars, with sweet food, drink, fruit and honour, surrounded by Brahmins and relatives, and the offering is eaten with respect. The Lord vanishes. The Brahmin and his wife do as told, call relatives and friends, and the Brahmin asks for happiness here and hereafter. He receives a chariot, an elephant, a house and a horse. They bow to the ground and receive the offering, and he spreads the worship of Satya Narayana in the world.

06-026.json.summary: Suta tells of a calm, gentle, wise king devoted to Narayana, Chandrachuda of Manipura, who fights a dreadful battle with proud foreigners. His great army goes to Yama's city, and five thousand footmen die and go to heaven. Overcome by the foreigners, he goes to Kashi on the pretext of a pilgrimage. He sees the city rich in wealth and grain, is amazed, and, seeing the Brahmin Sadananda who worships the true god, bows to him. Sadananda describes the Satya Narayana vow: gateways and plantain pillars, a lovely altar built by Brahmins in the middle, and worship with perfumes and flowers with love and devotion. The king worships in Kashi, takes a sword that destroys the enemy's side, kills six thousand bandits, and gains great wealth. By keeping the vow on every full-moon day, he becomes lord of a hundred thousand villages.

06-027.json.summary: Suta tells that some hunters go to Kashi to sell wood from the forest. They see Hari, served by Brahmins, and a Brahmin once seen as poor now seen as very rich, and ask how he got his wealth. Sadananda tells them of the Satya Narayana worship and the history of how a Nishada came to his hermitage. The rule is: wheat flour with ghee, bathing the god with the five nectars, and worship with sandal and others with fruit, flowers, incense and lamps. Pure devotion pleases him more than many things. He left the honour offered by Duryodhana, and ate the rice grains of Sudama. A cowherd, a vulture, a merchant, a hunter, Hanuman and Vibhishana reached him and are happy still. The hunters sell the wood, worship with the proceeds, bow at the end of the story and take the offering. By the power of the worship they gain children and wives and enjoy pleasures, and the poor and blind are said to gain as they wish.

06-028.json.summary: Suta tells of King Chandrachuda of Manipura and, in the city of Ratnapura, a merchant (Sadhu) who owns a hundred thousand. He sees many people at a river shore, rests his boat to see the wonder, and asks what they are doing. They say the worship of the true god gives wealth, a son, and all wishes. He wishes for a child, goes home thinking of Hari, holds festivals, and then has a lotus-eyed daughter. A daughter is said to be ten years old before she is a young woman. He chooses a fitting groom and gives the daughter with Vedic sound and music. He treats his son-in-law like a son. He then leaves with ships on trade. While all sleep, thieves steal his great wealth. The king hears of the theft, is angry, and has the merchant and son-in-law arrested and chained for twelve months, as the god was hostile. They lament.

06-029.json.summary: Suta continues the merchant's story. When Hari is against one, he says, many hells await. The merchant's wife Kalavati and her daughter, without food or clothing, are in need, and a man, Shilapala, gives five coins. The king is taught by a Brahmin in a dream. The merchant and his son-in-law say they are not thieves, ask to be judged truly, and the minister speaks. They are freed with song and music. Later an ascetic tells the merchant that his wealth is not in the boats, and the merchant faints from worry. The ascetic says that when King Chandrachuda worshipped Satya Narayana, he did not honour him, so how can he prosper? The merchant asks forgiveness and the pleased Narayana grants his wish. Kalavati ignores the offering and hurries away, and her son-in-law sinks with the boat; she faints, and is told to take the offering quickly. By the power of the vow the merchant is blessed with sons and grandsons. This is called the best of vows.

06-030.json.summary: The sages ask Suta about the highest celibate life, and Suta says that in the terrible Kali age, there is no forest-dwelling stage and celibacy is seen only here and there. A man asks what stage and class will do him good, and decides to take a wife, thus praising Shiva, the auspicious one, with a hymn that salutes Nature, the mother of the great principle, who makes the pairs of opposites, and Ignorance and Purity. A Brahmin marries the goddess named Brahmacharini and gives the seasonal gift to his wife. The four Vedas are named. The son of the Yajurveda is the Mimamsa teacher, and Vararuchi, a favourite of the king, is the son of the Atharva Veda. The king honours them. Vyadi, Mimamsa and Panini each speak to Chandragupta, and Vararuchi speaks to the king of Magadha. The student with staff and the almsman is named, and Pitrisharma meditates on Damodara.

06-031.json.summary: Suta tells that Panini, ashamed, goes to other holy places, drinks the water at Kedara and meditates on Shiva. After ten days he lives on air for ten days and, hearing nectar-like words, praises the god with a choking voice: "salutation to Bharga, the destroyer of sin, endless and Creator", and asks him to give the root of knowledge. The god says that the mind is the great holy place in the lake of knowledge, with the water of truth removing the dirt of passion and hatred, which shows Brahman. Then Rudra vanishes and Panini goes home. After composing the Linga-sutra, he attains the highest liberation. The Ganga herself, the auspicious one made of all holy places, comes there.

06-032.json.summary: Suta tells that Bopadeva goes to lovely Vrindavana, served by cowherds and cowherd women, and at the end of a year Hari himself gives him the best knowledge, described by Shuka to the wise Vishnurata. At the end of the story the Lord Vishnu appears. Bopadeva says people tormented by hell are fulfilled through his name in the Kali age. The Lord says the world will be ruled by Buddhists, made of pride and hypocrisy. The goddess Shiva asks who the best god is and, hearing the answer, goes to a secret place where Chandisha, Ganesha, Nandin and Guha are. The god tells her a lovely story kept in his mind. A parrot in a hollow hears it, becomes long-lived, and gains the greatness of the Bhagavata. The goddess is told to go to the bank of the Narmada and recite the story, and to give it to a worthy Vishnu devotee. Bopadeva then vanishes.

06-033.json.summary: The sages ask by which hymn one gains the fruit of reciting the Vedas, and Suta tells a story. A Brahmin named Tripathin has a wife, Kamini. He goes to recite the Saptashati for a living and stays away for a month. She meets a hunter who lives by selling wood and conceives by him. After twelve years the cunning son, who has no Vedic learning, and his mother are driven out by the Brahmin. Living on the Vindhya mountain, they recite the Chandika text daily, and both live happily in a hunter's house in the forest. The son steals, takes a woman's ornaments, and once receives something taken from a Brahmin's clothes, but by the merit of reciting the text he turns to righteousness and becomes a pupil, reciting the letters of Shiva. A worm-like being comes out of him, burnt in many colours. He recites the Adi Charita and praises Annapurna with a hymn. After a hundred and eight recitations the goddess gives him the Rigveda and disappears. He becomes the priest for King Vikramaditya's sacrifice.

06-034.json.summary: Suta tells that a wicked man out of greed for meat ate pigs and village cocks, then human flesh, and gave up everything else. The fearful man has the Chandika recitation done. He becomes a Kshatriya king of Magadha again, remembers his past lives and follows Vedic duty. A sage gives the king the middle episode of the Devi Mahatmya, and the king worships the eternal Mahalakshmi daily. By the grace of Mahamaya the place becomes holy. After twelve years his teacher, devoted to Shakti, arrives, and the eternal goddess, mother of the world, appears. The king, great and fortunate, enjoys pleasures the gods desire. Suta says this is the fate of the Yajurveda as told, and the greatness described by the sage.

06-035.json.summary: Suta tells of a man who knows the Vedas and their branches and is devoted to the Gita. Once he goes on a pilgrimage, and at the end of the year he is won over by a devotee of the goddess. Patanjali praises her: "you are faith, understanding, memory, learning, and the one who does good". A disembodied voice says he will gain true knowledge by the power of her story. He goes to the temple of Vindhyavasini and gains the knowledge that is her grace and turns to Vishnu. He wears the upright mark, tilaka and a tulasi necklace, and recites the Mahabhashya joyfully to each person. Suta says this is the best prayer to recite and ends with a blessing: may all see good and none share in sorrow. The listener who is pure and hears the collection of histories is blessed.

07-001.json.summary: This chapter begins the fourth part of the Pratisarga. The sages ask about the play the Lord performed at that time. Suta says that in the great kalpa called Bhavishya, in the Vaivasvata age, the Pandavas defeated the proud Kauravas. At the end of a day Krishna, knowing the bad turn of time, asks Shiva to protect the Pandavas who are his devotees. At night Ashvatthama, Bhoja and Kripa come, and Ashvatthama kills with a sword given by Shiva. A charioteer of Dhrishtadyumna survives, frightened. Learning that Shiva has done wrong, Bhima and the others become angry and their weapons enter Shiva's body. Rudra curses them: "you are worshippers of Krishna and will be reborn in the Kali age and bear this fault". They take refuge in Hari and praise Rudra, and Shiva appears. Krishna says he gave the curse out of necessity and tells who will be born: Yudhishthira as Vatsaraja's son, Bhima as a foreigner, a part of Arjuna as a devotee, Nakula at Kanyakubja, Sahadeva, a part of Dhritarashtra at Ajmer, and Karna as Taraka. Mahavati is a lovely city made by Mayadevi, and a part of Krishna is born as Udayasimha. He says he will kill the kings of the fire line and establish Kali.

07-002.json.summary: Suta describes kings who taught the duties of kings, liberation and giving, and went to heaven after ruling thirty-six years. Vyasa says the sages of Naimisha, after twelve hundred years, rise at a divine pool and do bathing and meditation. They name the lands, from the west end of the Sindhu river to Setubandha in the south, Ajmer, Marudhanva, Avanti, Udupa, Vanga, Gauda and Magadha, where many languages and religions stand. Hearing of the ruin of duty, they come with many groups by the Himalaya and Sindhu routes. A grandson of Vikramaditya takes his father's kingdom, sets a boundary between the foreigners and Aryas, and makes a foreign settlement beyond the Sindhu. In the middle of the Huna country, a good man on a mountain tells the king that he teaches the foreigners' way, and that a fearful being called Ishamasi appeared among bandits at the decline of truth. He tells the king to recite a pure Vedic prayer and meditate on the Lord in the sun's disc. The king bows, regains his kingdom and performs a horse sacrifice.

07-003.json.summary: Suta tells that the limits of duty were slowly lost on earth. A king with ten thousand soldiers and Kalidasa conquers the foreigners of Gandhara, Kashmir and Narava. Another foreigner comes with a teacher, and King Bhoja prays to Mahadeva, "lord of Girija, dweller in the desert, hidden by foreigners, pure and of the form of being, consciousness and bliss". The land of Bahlika is polluted by foreigners, with a great magician whom the god had burnt earlier. The god tells the king not to go to the demon-like land. The king returns home. A man skilled in magic speaks to him lovingly and tells him to eat his leftovers. The king's mind turns to the foreign way. Kalidasa, angry, says he will kill the wicked Bahlika, recites ten thousand times and makes the fire offering. The frightened disciples go to Bahlika. At night a god-like man tells the king that his Aryan way is the best. He says those who are circumcised, shaveless, bearded and defile are different, and that animals should be eaten except by the Kaula rite. The king returns home and sets up the Prakrit language for Shudras and a boundary for the foreigners. People of Aryan classes stay beyond the Vindhyas, and mixed castes live in Barbara, Tushara and many islands.

07-004.json.summary: Suta says the earth had many kings in their kingdom, and three kings of their line died within two hundred years. The king ruled his own kingdom by duty at Kalpakshetra. In Indraprastha Anangapala of the Tomara family is named. The fire line grew stronger, from the north to the end of China and to Setubandha in the south, with fire-offering makers who care for cows and Brahmins. A time like the Dvapara age returns everywhere, with a god and a sacrifice in every village and land. Seeing this, the terrible Kali, afraid with Mleccha, practised meditation for twelve years. Kali praises Hari, who removes all sin and makes all time, saying he has lost his body, family and kingdom. Krishna, laughing, says a part of him will come to earth and destroy the mighty ones, and vanishes. A king keeps the nine-night Durga vow for nine years, and the goddess grants a boon. He marries by duty and settles her at home. Acharya, Vatsaraja, a foreigner called Shatayatta and the mighty Talana are named. A battle of the two kings is dreadful, and then they make friendship with Talana.

07-005.json.summary: Suta tells of the birth of two girls by Shiva's favour, for King Someshvara of the Chauhan family. A Brahmin, Jayasharma, is in trance on the Himalaya, gives up his body, and a part of Nakula is born on earth by Shiva's command. He conquers Gauda, Vanga and others and the proud desert lands. Three proud sons are born to Kirtimalini, and Simhakhela at twelve years. Dhundhukara rules at Mathura and his younger brother at Ajmer. A strong son of Pradyota named Parimala is born, and Bhishmasimha, lord of elephants, from Vidyota. Seeing those unfriendly to him, he drives them from his kingdom. A bold son who gained his maternal grandfather's kingdom is told by those he has driven out how he can enjoy all the kingdom. King Jayachandra says "Parimala, you are brave, be my minister now". They are glad. A fort city is built, and Delhi is founded at a good time at the fort's gate, and the king, amazed, names it Delhi. After three years Jayachandra asks Prithviraj why he did not give his share, and sends a messenger. A proud king says he drove out the cunning men of the moon line and gathered sixteen hundred thousand troops, and that the strong king must pay tax. Jayachandra, afraid of Prithviraj, is shown, and Prithviraj takes half the kingdom.

07-006.json.summary: Suta tells that Mahiraja (Prithviraj) is amazed at the news. A woman named Tilaka is named. A Gauda king's daughter, Divyavibhavari, has a daughter, Samyogini. At Kanyakubja a golden image of Kamakshi is set up. The goddess says to a father that if he worships this yogini she will be dear to him. Five thousand chariots with archers, Dhundhukara, lord of elephants, and eight hundred thousand horses are named. The army stretches twenty krosha. On the far bank of the Ishani river, a palanquin is placed. Pradyota and Vidyota guard Ratnabhanu. Horses die by horses and elephants by elephants. The battle lasts five days with great loss of heroes. A hundred thousand horses die and go to heaven. Dhundhukara strikes Pradyota in the heart with arrows, three spears fell him to the ground, and a spear kills him and he goes to heaven. Lakshana, with them, fights angrily. The two equal heroes fight on elephants. When the mighty one is killed, the people of Kanyakubja flee in fear of Mahiraja, to their homes. Prithviraj wins, and Jayachandra's fame in battle is told. Jayachandra rules at Kanyakubja and Prithviraj at Delhi.

07-007.json.summary: Suta tells that Bhishmasimha, on the Ganga's bank in the sign of Leo, worships Indra, and after a month Indra, knowing his devotion, gives him gifts and vanishes. At that time Parimala, grieving for his father, goes to Kashi to die with his wife. A serpent at a root tells the Rudra serpent that he is cruel and slow-witted, and he has been glad in the king's body every day. A fool king, it says, is the one who does not give hot oil. The king does what the serpent said and is freed of disease. At midnight in the darkness, a sun appears in all directions, and he praises Shiva with the Mahimna hymn. Mahadeva takes the form of a linga. Malkhana, pleased, comes to Mahavati and goes to Jayachandra's city after a year. Lakshana, a hero, prays to the lord of Usha. Within a fortnight Vishnu, the lord of the world, answers, and Lakshana goes home on the elephant Airavati. They live together in friendship. A group says they will go to their cities, and the king agrees. Karinari, Sulalita and others are named. Talana is a hero at his son's command, dear to Rakshasas, and two sons of Vasuman are named. The king is given a five-voiced great serpent from Indra and a horse, Papiha, a gift of the sun, with a human voice. The army is sixty thousand, with Talana as its lord. Protected by these heroes the king is fulfilled.

07-008.json.summary: Suta tells how a king worships Shiva with earth images, and the god offers a boon, which the king asks for with folded hands. Mahadeva grants it and vanishes. A strong man, going to deliver a message, says he will go with the troops to the pure Ganga, and speaks to his sister, who wants victory; she gives a jewelled necklace. Kaliya comes quickly with a hundred thousand horses. After giving gifts to Brahmins he goes to Jayachandra's city. A strong man who got a boon from Shiva goes to lovely Mahavati and takes refuge in Rudra, Shambhu with matted hair. A great battle lasting a day and night follows with Vatsaraja, who has sixteen thousand horses, and the heroes of both armies fall. They destroy the enemy army and cry out in victory. Kaliya is defeated, Bhishmasimha rouses the soldiers and strikes an enemy with an arrow named Bhairava, the army of Mahishmati scatters in ten directions, and a king cuts off his head. King Parimala and Jayachandra are amazed at the enemy's defeat. Five months after Bhishmasimha's death, a part of Sahadeva is born on earth by Shiva's command, and the king gives much wealth at the news.

07-009.json.summary: Suta tells of a thousand-fold Chandika fire offering and a meeting of many kings. Two heroes had been bound each day by the king's daughters. Devaki is given to Desharaja and Brahmi to his younger brother, with a hundred elephants, five chariots, a thousand horses, servants and much wealth. When a son is born, Devaki conceives again. The baby is known as a part of Rama, with a cheerful face. A month later Brahmi bears a son, and the Brahmins, seeing him, are glad. At three years Balakhani is born, and Chamunda, Devaki's son, is named as a danger to his own line. Jambuka comes with his troops against Vatsaraja, and a great battle with seven hundred thousand men of Mahishmati follows. By Shiva's boon, the brothers are defeated. The enemy burns the whole city and goes home. A goddess's favourite carries a seven-month part of Krishna and, in the land of Kalpa, sets him in the Yamuna. On the eighth of the dark fortnight of Bhadrapada, the dark-limbed, lotus-eyed boy shining like a sapphire is born, and a voice from the sky says that Udaya has been born as the sun among gods. Brahmi bears a strong son, a part of an attendant. The children grow, and at three years the strong part of Krishna and the divine mare Ashvini and Harini near Uchchaihshravas are mentioned. At eight Krishna's part does the name ceremony.

07-010.json.summary: Suta tells how the code of duty became the best of all. A king sends his army to Mahavati for tribute, and the people there are told to give a sixth as a tax to the king. The king hears and sends a lakh of heroes to Kanyakubja. Many local rulers are in his land, and Mahiraja, hearing this, is greatly afraid. The son of the lord of Urvi, a strong sixteen-year-old, is mentioned, and a king speaks lovingly to his nephew, asking him to wrestle. Astrologers are called and the time asked. The northern Naimisharanya becomes his own country. Hearing this, Krishna's part is hurt by words like arrows. Seeing his son faint, the king takes a sword in hand, and another king stops him. The boy bows to the father. The chapter then tells of the mare Harini and the gift of Indra to Bhishmasimha. The sages ask about Harini, and Suta tells the earlier story: King Desharaja, a pious man, asks a boon, and from that union horses are born. Harini gives birth to Megha and Pushpa and Balahaka. A tiger, terror of beings, is killed by Ahlada. The goddess Sharada, fair-faced, is mentioned, and says "remember me when you are afraid" and vanishes. The king sees their valour and is glad.

07-011.json.summary: Suta tells that the heroes stay in a vow in the month of Madhava, worshipping with seasonal flowers, incense and lamps. The goddess gives a boon, and they go home, their purpose achieved. In Ashadha, Krishna's part, riding a horse, gives gold to the twice-born. At the king's order warriors try to bind him, but the hero is awakened by divine illusion. Women, seeing his lovely form, try to charm him. Hearing a piteous word, he leaves his city. When Krishna's part is eleven and fierce in battle, his sister sees her brother distressed and tells him something, calling Dhundhukara. Devasimha, who knows the time, hears the enemy is coming and says he will deal with Mahiraja and Dhundhukara with their troops. The enemy arrive with four hundred thousand soldiers and make a loud noise. Sixty thousand of the army go to heaven. Horses fight horses and camels fight camel riders. Brahmananda sends enemies to Yama's house with arrows. Seeing his army beaten, the strong Dhundhukara is wounded on an elephant and faints. A strong man, with a boon from Shiva, comes riding an elephant, worships his guns and makes a great slaughter. He makes Mahiraja and his relatives with their mounts faint and binds Sukhakhani and others in strong chains. Balakhani goes by Devasimha's order. King Parimala comes gladly and returns home with Brahmananda.

07-012.json.summary: Suta tells how at lovely Kanyakubja many kings come together with armies. Jambuka, a king with the people of the Narmada, is named. Krishna's part speaks quickly to his mother. Talana comes quickly with four hundred thousand troops. Flags of five thousand and a thousand woodcutters are mentioned. They bow to King Malana and give many gifts. Seeing his mother deluded, they are glad. Krishna's part speaks softly to a woman, dances, and Balakhani sings. A courtesan, learning her son Ahlada has become a yogi, sees the heroes bound and shuts a door to bind them. The two armies meet to fight. Seeing his army broken, Kaliya goes to Balakhani, and Suryavarman, learning his relative Kaliya is bound, comes. The great battle lasts many days with heroes of Mahishmati and Rankana. Talana is the angry commander every day. A woman skilled in illusion goes to comfort her father, and uses a Rakshasi's illusion. A prince who was a great demon named Chitra in a past life is named. King Jambuka, with a boon from Shiva, is bound with strong iron chains. The goddess Devaki, devoted to her husband, kills the enemy's sons, and orders Jambuka's body crushed with oils she has made. All the soldiers return to Mahavati, joyful and fulfilled.

07-013.json.summary: The sages ask, and Suta tells that a king offers wealth of half a crore. Krishna's part sits on Bindula and Vatsaja on Harini. At the full moon when Rahu seizes the moon in darkness, he gives the nectar-drum to the king and speaks again. Netrasimha, who looked after him like a son, is named. Two friends come in palanquins to the king. A woman worships Durga and recites the middle episode of the Chandi. A man goes to the flower-garden in Mahavati. A man says his father, enemy by Indra's boon, is such. On the fifth of the dark fortnight of Magha, he tells him to come quickly with signs of battle on his body. He speaks to the mighty king Netrasimha, who faints with anger. Netrasimha with kings of the hills fights a dreadful battle. Krishna's part, on a divine horse, comforts them. He worships the giver of all wishes with the music of the nectar-drum. A father says he has seen the same in a dream. The maiden is meant for a famous part of Rama. The enemy are told that they are Aryan Abhiras and that they will perish with their families like Jambuka. A thousand kings are placed in a tent with their forces. Sukhakhani blocks the victory at the third turn. Balakhani takes Harini, Harinagara is mentioned, and Netrasimha, the fine brother, king of Sundara forest. Messengers on camels bring news, and King Malana holds a great festival in every house.

07-014.json.summary: Suta says that on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra, at noon on a Thursday, a best of sons is born, and the gods with sages come. Ahlada, gladly, has the birth rites for the child performed. Indula is born as a son, and after two months a hundred troops of dancers with songs are mentioned on earth. Yogasimha stays seven nights and goes home. Out of love for the boy he takes him away by his magic, and Shachi gives the child her own breast. The moon takes the house of nectar in his own body. When the child is lost, Goddess Svarnavati and Ahlada learn what happened in the ten villages, and Ahlada with his family fasts and controls his senses. The pleased goddess speaks as a disembodied voice: Jayanta, Indra's son, has gone to heaven. As long as Ahlada stayed on earth, the boy would stay on earth. Hearing this, they were free of grief.

07-015.json.summary: Suta tells that after reciting the Saptashati at the three twilights with love and devotion, a Brahmin's son named Chamunda, born to Samanta, grew famous. At twelve, after reading the three-part text, he says he will fill a vessel for devotees. Sukhakhani brings honey, flowers and fruit, and Devaki honours the goddess with offerings and sandal. Ahlada bows with his whole body and Udaya with his head. The goddess, loving her devotees, speaks to them. She says the great hero Balakhani will die after a long time, Devaki will be a goddess and go to her own world for a long time, and Devasimha, free of desire, will gain liberation when he dies.

07-016.json.summary: Suta tells that when King Ratnabhanu dies, the king of Marudhanva comes. The Lord is pleased and gives a fine horse, Pavakiya, a horse of fire. The men are eighteen years old.
